itemListElement.name: Salmon Orzo with Dill and Capers for Two

@graph.name: Salmon Orzo with Dill and Capers for Two
recipeIngredient: 1/2 teaspoon Diamond Crystal kosher salt, divided
1/4 cup dry white wine or low-sodium chicken broth
1 cup low-sodium chicken or vegetable broth
2 tablespoons finely chopped fresh dill, plus more for garnish

recipeInstructions.name: Pat salmon fillets completely dry with paper towels
recipeInstructions.text: Pat salmon fillets completely dry with paper towels. Season all over with half the salt and all the pepper. Let sit at room temperature while you prep the other ingredients.

recipeInstructions.name: Heat olive oil in a 10-inch stainless steel or carbon steel skillet over…
recipeInstructions.text: Heat olive oil in a 10-inch stainless steel or carbon steel skillet over medium-high until shimmering. Carefully lay salmon skin-side down in the pan. Press gently with a spatula for 10 seconds to ensure full skin contact. Cook undisturbed for 4–5 minutes until skin is deep golden and you can see the edges of the flesh turning opaque about halfway up the side. Flip and cook 1–2 minutes more until an instant-read thermometer inserted in the thickest part registers 145°F / 63°C. Transfer to a plate, skin-side up, and tent loosely with foil.

recipeInstructions.name: Reduce heat to medium
recipeInstructions.text: Reduce heat to medium. Melt 1 tablespoon butter in the same skillet. Add shallot and cook, stirring, until softened, about 1 minute. Add garlic and cook until fragrant, 30 seconds. Stir in orzo and toast, stirring often, until the grains smell nutty and look slightly translucent at the edges, about 1–2 minutes until the internal temperature reaches 165°F / 74°C on an instant-read thermometer.

recipeInstructions.name: Pour in wine, using a wooden spoon to scrape up any browned bits from the…
recipeInstructions.text: Pour in wine, using a wooden spoon to scrape up any browned bits from the bottom of the pan (that's pure flavor). Cook until the liquid is nearly evaporated, about 30 seconds. Add broth and frozen peas, bring to a brisk simmer, then reduce heat to maintain a gentle bubble. Cook, stirring occasionally, until orzo is tender and the mixture has thickened to a creamy, risotto-like consistency, 8–10 minutes. If it dries before the orzo is done, add a splash of water.

recipeInstructions.name: Remove the pan from heat
recipeInstructions.text: Remove the pan from heat. Stir in capers, lemon juice, lemon zest, fresh dill, and remaining 1 tablespoon butter until melted and glossy. Taste and adjust seasoning with the remaining salt if needed.

recipeInstructions.name: Spoon the creamy orzo onto two warm plates
recipeInstructions.text: Spoon the creamy orzo onto two warm plates. Top each with a salmon fillet, skin-side up so the crisp skin stays crackly. Finish with a sprinkle of extra dill, a lemon wedge on the side, and a few scattered capers. Serve immediately.

mainEntity.name: How long does salmon orzo with dill and capers last in the fridge?

acceptedAnswer.text: Stored in an airtight container, this dish will keep for up to 2 days. The orzo will absorb more liquid overnight, so it will be thicker when you reheat it. Warm it gently in a skillet over low heat, adding a tablespoon of water at a time until it loosens up. I do not recommend microwaving; it overcooks the salmon and turns the orzo gummy. The crisp skin won't survive storage, so plan for tender flakes instead.

mainEntity.name: Can you freeze salmon orzo with dill and capers?

acceptedAnswer.text: Freezing isn't ideal. Orzo tends to turn mushy upon thawing, and salmon can develop a fishy off-taste. If you must freeze, pack into a freezer-safe container and use within 1 month. Thaw overnight in the refrigerator and reheat on the stovetop with a splash of water. The texture won't be the same — expect a creamy porridge rather than distinct grains — but the lemon-dill-caper flavor will still be there.

mainEntity.name: What do you serve with salmon orzo with dill and capers?

acceptedAnswer.text: Because the orzo already bundles starch, vegetable, and sauce into one pan, I keep the side minimal. A simple arugula salad dressed with olive oil and lemon juice balances the richness beautifully. If you want something warm, quick-sautéed asparagus or green beans with a little garlic would echo the flavors without adding work. A chilled glass of unoaked Chardonnay or a dry rosé is my standard pour.

mainEntity.name: How can I tell when the salmon is done without a thermometer?

acceptedAnswer.text: Press the thickest part of the fillet gently with your finger. If it feels firm and starts to flake along the natural lines of the muscle, it's at or near 145°F. The flesh should be opaque and you'll see a bit of white albumin between the flakes. But an instant-read thermometer is the most reliable tool. I keep one clipped to my apron — it's a $12 guarantee against overcooked fish.

mainEntity.name: What are common mistakes when making this for two?

acceptedAnswer.text: Overcrowding the pan is the biggest one. A 10-inch skillet fits two salmon fillets comfortably, but if you shove them in without enough space, the temperature drops and the skin steams instead of sears. The second most frequent mistake is adding the orzo to cold broth and expecting a creamy sauce — you must bring the liquid to a simmer before the starch starts to release. Finally, forgetting to tent the salmon while the orzo cooks means the fillet cools too quickly; a loose foil cover traps just enough heat without softening the skin.
